catalog_quote: Alex (1989:24) remarks that “all Central Delta lects operate a basic two-tone system”. These tones are low tone, which is marked with a grave accent ( ̀), and high tone, which is marked with an acute accent ( ´). There is also a downstep phenomenon in these languages. The downstep is marked with a small arrow pointing downwards ( ꜜ) between two high-toned syllables. Apart from the syllabic nasal, tone in these languages is anchored on vowels. Table 7 shows these tones and downstep as found in Abuan, Oḍual and Ogbrọnụagum. ... Like in lexical items, tone can distinguish grammatical constructions in Central Delta languages. new_statements.rule_in_words: Obulom, like the other Central Delta languages, is described as a two-tone language (High vs Low, with downstepped High); tone is lexically and grammatically contrastive. No source examined says anything about word stress or accent placement; the tone statement itself is a group-level generalisation (quoting Alex 1989) in a comparative overview that explicitly includes Obulom among the six languages surveyed, not an Obulom-specific description.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Kari's tone illustrations are from Abuan, Odual and Ogbronuagum only; no Obulom tone examples beyond tone-marked lexical items (numerals p.4, verbal extensions Table). Kari 2019 (Marang 31, p.11) independently states that in all Rivers State languages (Obulom included) pitch distinguishes words, phrases and sentences. The UCLA 1994 Ladefoged/Williamson field sheet marks H/L/falling tones and queries downstep on Obulom items.
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical and grammatical tone at word level; nothing on phrase-level prominence or citation-form accent. Coverage is Obulom (Abuloma) only; Ochichi (moribund co-dialect, ochi1235) is excluded from Kari's phonological discussion for lack of data.
new_statements.identity_note: obul1239 'Obulom-Ochichi' groups Obulom proper (Abuloma town, Port Harcourt LGA; Glottolog dialect obul1238, ISO obu, c. 3,400 speakers) with moribund Ochichi (Ikwerengwo and Umuebulu, Etche LGA; ochi1235, ISO xoc). Everything found concerns Obulom/Abuloma only; Ochichi is known from a 100-word 1981 typescript and five numerals (Ndimele 2003) and is excluded from all phonological discussion. The tone statement quoted is a Central Delta group-level generalisation (Kari 2017 quoting Alex 1989), not an Obulom-specific description.

sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent. Sec. 3.4 'Tone' (p.11): all Central Delta lects (Obulom is one of the six languages surveyed, data from Ngeripaka 2000) operate a basic two-tone system, H and L, plus downstep; tone anchored on vowels and syllabic nasals; tone also distinguishes grammatical constructions. Tone examples given only for Abuan, Odual, Ogbronuagum. Obulom-specific content: 20 vowels, 22 consonants, verbal extensions, numerals.
